blocks.text:
We know that \(\sinh x = \frac{e^{x}-e^{-x}}{2}\). This can be written as
\[\sinh x = \dfrac{e^{x} - \frac{1}{e^{x}}}{2} = \dfrac{e^{x} - \left(\frac{1}{e}\right)^{x}}{2}\]
Since domain of \(e^{x}\) and \(\left(\frac{1}{e}\right)^{x}\) is \(\mathbb{R}\), therefore, the domain of \(\sinh x\) is \(\mathbb{R} = (-\infty, \infty)\).

As \(x \to \infty\), \(e^{x} \to \infty\) and \(\left(\frac{1}{e}\right)^{x} \to 0\). Hence, \(\sinh x = \frac{e^{x} - (1/e)^{x}}{2} \to \infty\).
As \(x \to -\infty\), \(e^{x} \to 0\) and \(\left(\frac{1}{e}\right)^{x} \to \infty\). Hence, \(\sinh x = \frac{e^{x} - (1/e)^{x}}{2} \to -\infty\).
Therefore, the range of \(\sinh x\) is \(\mathbb{R} = (-\infty, \infty)\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why write \(e^{-x}\) as \(\left(\frac{1}{e}\right)^{x}\)? Because then both parts are exponential functions \(a^{x}\) from section 1.4: \(e^{x}\) with base \(e > 1\) (increasing) and \(\left(\frac{1}{e}\right)^{x}\) with base \(\frac{1}{e} < 1\) (decreasing). Their known behaviour at \(\pm\infty\) gives the behaviour of \(\sinh x\).
Why is the range all of \(\mathbb{R}\)? \(\sinh x\) is continuous, goes down to \(-\infty\) on the left and up to \(\infty\) on the right, so it takes every real value on the way. It is also strictly increasing (an increasing \(e^{x}\) minus a decreasing \(e^{-x}\)), so each value is taken exactly once. This is why \(\sinh x\) has an inverse (page 1.5.4).
At \(x = 0\), \(\sinh 0 = \frac{e^{0} - e^{-0}}{2} = 0\), so the graph of \(\sinh x\) passes through the point \((0, 0)\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The table and Figure 1.8 print \(\sinh 3\) as 10.03 (and \(\sinh(-3)\) as \(-10.03\)). The correct value is
\[\sinh 3 = \dfrac{e^{3} - e^{-3}}{2}\]
\[\approx \dfrac{20.0855 - 0.0498}{2}\]
\[\approx 10.0179 \approx 10.02\]
So the entries should be 10.02 and \(-10.02\). (Do not confuse it with \(\cosh 3 \approx 10.07\).) Our figure plots 10.02.
The graph of \(\sinh x\) is shown in Figure 1.8.

blocks.alt: Graph of y = sinh x on axes from x = minus 3 to 3 and y = minus 12 to 12. The curve rises from bottom left to top right through the origin, with plotted points (minus 3, minus 10.02), (minus 2, minus 3.63), (minus 1, minus 1.18), (0, 0), (1, 1.18), (2, 3.63) and (3, 10.02).
blocks.caption: Figure 1.8: the graph of y = sinh x (original drawing after the textbook's figure; sinh 3 plotted as 10.02)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Notice the symmetry in the table: \(\sinh(-x) = -\sinh x\) (the values for \(-1, -2, -3\) are the negatives of those for \(1, 2, 3\)). Such a function is called odd, and its graph is symmetric about the origin: turn Figure 1.8 upside down (rotate it by \(180^{\circ}\)) and it looks the same.
Proof: \(\sinh(-x) = \frac{e^{-x} - e^{x}}{2} = -\frac{e^{x} - e^{-x}}{2} = -\sinh x\).

We know that \(\cosh x = \frac{e^{x}+e^{-x}}{2}\). This can be written as
\[\cosh x = \dfrac{e^{x} + \frac{1}{e^{x}}}{2} = \dfrac{e^{x} + \left(\frac{1}{e}\right)^{x}}{2}\]
Since domain of \(e^{x}\) and \(\left(\frac{1}{e}\right)^{x}\) is \(\mathbb{R}\), therefore, the domain of \(\cosh x\) is \(\mathbb{R} = (-\infty, \infty)\).

As \(x \to \infty\), \(e^{x} \to \infty\) and \(\left(\frac{1}{e}\right)^{x} \to 0\). Hence, \(\cosh x = \frac{e^{x} + (1/e)^{x}}{2} \to \infty\).
As \(x \to -\infty\), \(e^{x} \to 0\) and \(\left(\frac{1}{e}\right)^{x} \to \infty\). Hence, \(\cosh x = \frac{e^{x} + (1/e)^{x}}{2} \to \infty\).

At \(x = 0\), \(\cosh 0 = \frac{e^{0} + e^{-0}}{2} = 1\), so the graph of \(\cosh x\) passes through the point \((0, 1)\) and \(y = 1\) is minimum value of the graph. Therefore, the range of \(\cosh x\) is \([1, \infty)\). To sketch the graph, we take a table of values:

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is 1 the smallest value? A square is never negative:
\[\left(e^{x/2} - e^{-x/2}\right)^{2} \ge 0\]
\[e^{x} - 2 + e^{-x} \ge 0\]
\[\dfrac{e^{x} + e^{-x}}{2} \ge 1\]
So \(\cosh x \ge 1\) for every \(x\), with equality only when \(e^{x/2} = e^{-x/2}\), i.e. \(x = 0\). Both ends go to \(\infty\), so the range is exactly \([1, \infty)\).
The graph of \(\cosh x\) is shown in Figure 1.9.

blocks.alt: Graph of y = cosh x on axes from x = minus 4 to 4 and y = 0 to 11. A U-shaped curve with lowest point (0, 1), symmetric about the y-axis, through (plus or minus 1, 1.54), (plus or minus 2, 3.76) and (plus or minus 3, 10.07).
blocks.caption: Figure 1.9: the graph of y = cosh x (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Here the table shows \(\cosh(-x) = \cosh x\): the same values on both sides. Such a function is called even, and its graph is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis (fold Figure 1.9 along the \(y\)-axis and the two halves match). Proof: \(\cosh(-x) = \frac{e^{-x} + e^{x}}{2} = \cosh x\).
Because every height above 1 is reached twice (once at \(x\) and once at \(-x\)), \(\cosh x\) is not one-to-one on \(\mathbb{R}\). This is why its inverse needs a restricted domain (page 1.5.4).

blocks.caption: sinh x and cosh x side by side
rows: Odd: \(\sinh(-x) = -\sinh x\), symmetric about the origin
Decreasing on \((-\infty, 0]\), increasing on \([0, \infty)\); not one-to-one

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\sinh x\): domain and range \(\mathbb{R}\), through \((0, 0)\), odd, strictly increasing (one-to-one).
2. \(\cosh x\): domain \(\mathbb{R}\), range \([1, \infty)\), lowest point \((0, 1)\), even, not one-to-one on \(\mathbb{R}\).
3. Behaviour at the ends comes from \(e^{x} \to \infty, e^{-x} \to 0\) as \(x \to \infty\), and the reverse as \(x \to -\infty\).
4. Plot with a table: \(\sinh 1 \approx 1.18\), \(\sinh 2 \approx 3.63\), \(\sinh 3 \approx 10.02\); \(\cosh 1 \approx 1.54\), \(\cosh 2 \approx 3.76\), \(\cosh 3 \approx 10.07\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Drawing \(\cosh x\) through the origin: it starts at \((0, 1)\) because \(e^{0} + e^{0} = 2\), and \(2/2 = 1\).
2. Drawing \(\cosh x\) as a parabola \(y = x^{2} + 1\): near 0 they look alike, but \(\cosh x\) grows much faster (at \(x = 3\) it is 10.07, the parabola gives 10, and at \(x = 5\) it is about 74.2 against 26).
3. Giving \(\sinh x\) a minimum or a maximum: it has neither; it keeps rising.
4. Writing the range of \(\cosh x\) as \((1, \infty)\): the value 1 is reached at \(x = 0\), so the bracket is closed.
